title: Tenali Raman and the False Rain Astrologer
summary: During an anxious dry spell before the arrival of the monsoon, a self-proclaimed 'Supreme Imperial Astrologer' named Varahamitra set up camp near Vijayanagara. He held up a drie...
keywords: the trick of the palm leaf
full_text:
During an anxious dry spell before the arrival of the monsoon, a self-proclaimed 'Supreme Imperial Astrologer' named Varahamitra set up camp near Vijayanagara. He held up a dried palm leaf covered in mysterious astrological diagrams and declared:
'According to my celestial calculations, an evil planetary conjunction has blocked the rain clouds over Vijayanagara!
Unless the Emperor and the farming guilds pay five thousand gold coins to perform a seven-day Celestial Cloud Sacrifice, not a single drop of rain will fall, and the entire empire will perish in famine!'

Terrified farmers sold their cattle to contribute to the sacrifice fund.
King Krishnadevaraya was on the verge of handing over the gold when Tenali Raman intervened:
'Maharaj, let me examine the astrologer’s palm leaf. If his celestial calculations are infallible, he should be able to predict today’s local atmospheric events with absolute precision.'

Tenali approached the astrologer and asked:
'Revered Astrologer, does your palm leaf reveal what the sky will drop upon your own head before this afternoon’s audience concludes?'
The astrologer puffed out his chest:
'The stars reveal only celestial truths! The sky will drop nothing upon my head today, for the atmosphere is dry as bone!'

Tenali nodded. He stepped to the palace balcony, gave a prearranged signal to his servants waiting on the roof directly above the assembly terrace.
Within three seconds, a massive, fifty-gallon leather fire bucket filled with cold, muddy river water was dumped straight down upon the astrologer's head!
*SPLAAASH!*

The astrologer was knocked to his knees, his tall silk turban crushed, his face dripping with muddy slime, his astrology palm leaf soaked into pulp!
He spluttered and shrieked in fury:
'Treason! Outrage! Who dumped this filthy water on my head?'

Tenali Raman folded his hands with innocent courtesy:
'Alas, great Astrologer! You claimed to know the movements of clouds across ten thousand leagues of heaven, yet you could not predict a local rainstorm occurring three feet above your own head!
If your stars cannot warn you of a simple bucket of river water, how can you demand five thousand gold coins to predict the monsoon?'

The King and the entire court erupted in laughter.
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the charlatan to return every coin to the farmers and banished him from the empire.
Three days later, natural monsoon clouds gathered over the Western Ghats, bringing torrential, life-giving rain to the fertile fields of Vijayanagara, proving that nature follows its eternal laws, not the greed of false prophets.
moral: Superstitious prophecies designed to fleece anxious farmers crumble before empirical observation.
